newsitem.title: UK: It's still wait-and-see on Euro currency.
newsitem.headline: It's still wait-and-see on Euro currency.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major stuck to his wait-and-see policy on the European Union's planned single currency amid speculation that his finance minister would have resigned if he had changed his stance.
Major told parliament the position had not changed, dismissing suggestions he would give in to "Euro-sceptics" and promise that he would keep Britain out of the Euro currency.
Britain must have a general election by next May and many "Euro-sceptic" Conservatives believe that to rule out being among the first entrants to the new currency could win votes.
In response to a question from Labour opposition leader Tony Blair asking if the policy was the same, Major said: "That remains unequivocally the position."

This was seen as a victory for Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke and Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine, pro-European members of Major's cabinet, and a blow to "Euro-sceptics" whose resistance to further integration with Europe has split the ruling Conservatives.
"Skewered," said a headline in the top-selling newspaper The Sun, which added: "Heseltine and Ken ambush PM to stop him saving the pound."

It said the two had made Major rule out promising not to scrap the pound. Major has a one-seat majority in parliament and their resignations could have plunged the Conservatives into a disastrous early election.

"The agreement between the two most senior member of Mr. Major's government, and the rare clarity of Mr. Major's (House of) Commons answers, fuelled Tory Euro-sceptic and Labour suspicions that Mr Major had been bullied into submission on pain of joint resignation," said The Independent.
The Times also suggested that Clarke would have gone if Major had altered his policy.
"By last night, the policy of keeping open options on the single currency appeared to be set in stone, much firmer than it had been," it said.
One disgruntled Euro-sceptic told The Express that Major's latest move could have cost the party the election.
"This is consigning us to election defeat. The polls aren't moving, the budget has not worked and we are now throwing away our last trump card."
The latest opinion poll published on Tuesday showed Labour had increased its lead over the ruling Conservatives to 19 from 13 percentage points.
Rumours that Major was about to harden his position surfaced on Monday and led to Heseltine telling BBC radio that government policy had not changed.
"This has been a bad day," a ministerial aide told The Times. "John Major has been kidnapped by Clarke and Heseltine. They are yesterday's men fighting yesterday's battles."
